notes.b: A multinational company (MNC) is a company based in one home country that runs production or service branches in several other countries. The syllabus asks you to study one MNC to understand how it is structured and organised, so the general pattern comes first.
points: Definition: a company with its headquarters (the main control centre) in its home country and production or service branches in several host countries (the countries that receive the branches). It is also called a transnational corporation (TNC).

Typical structure: headquarters, research and development (R&D, the work of inventing and designing new products) and top management stay in the home country as the core. Branch plants, regional headquarters, and sales and service offices are placed abroad.
Decisions are made at headquarters, and branch plants compete with each other inside the company for investment, so a plant that is less efficient or more costly risks losing out to another.

Production is split into stages: design and R&D; basic processing of raw materials and components; assembly and testing; distribution and sales. Each stage is placed where it is cheapest or most efficient, which spreads sourcing, basic processing and markets across the world.

The largest MNCs have sales or market values (the total worth of the company's shares) greater than the gross domestic product (GDP, the value of all goods and services a country produces in a year) of many countries, and they control much of world trade and investment.
The largest companies by market value in the mid-2020s are American technology companies: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google's parent) and Amazon.
notes.tip: Exams use a chart or table of the largest MNCs by value. You may be asked to draw a bar chart and calculate differences, so know the skill at the end of this subsection. Do not copy company values from past-paper charts.

notes.h: Foreign direct investment and IDA Ireland
notes.b: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by a company in another country, made by building or buying a plant there. Ireland has a State agency whose job is to win this investment.
points: IDA Ireland (Industrial Development Authority), set up in 1949, is the State agency responsible for attracting and keeping FDI, so it is the body that supports foreign companies both before and after they arrive.

IDA client companies employ about 300,000 people in about 1,800 companies (2023-24), concentrated in the Dublin region, which has the largest labour pool, universities, Dublin Port and Airport, services and existing clusters of firms.

Other Irish-based MNCs: Pfizer (Ringaskiddy, Co. Cork, and Grange Castle, Dublin), Google (European headquarters, Barrow Street, Dublin), Meta (international headquarters, Dublin), Microsoft (in Ireland since 1985) and Dell (Limerick).
notes.tip: A data response on IDA Ireland can ask what IDA stands for, one of its roles, and why the Dublin and Mid-East region has the most jobs in foreign-owned firms.

notes.b: Ireland has no shortage of competition for foreign investment, so a company needs reasons to build here. These are the MNC-specific advantages of Ireland, and each one can be developed into an explained point.
points: Low corporation tax (the tax a company pays on its profits) of 12.5%, rising to 15% for very large multinational groups (turnover over 750 million euro) from 2024 under the OECD global minimum tax agreement.
A young, educated, English-speaking workforce, which suits high-skill and customer-facing work.
EU membership, which Ireland joined in 1973 as the EEC (now the EU), gives access to the single market (one trading area with no tariffs between members).
Since the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, Ireland is the only euro-area country where English is the main language (Malta also has English as an official language).
IDA grants and support for companies that invest here, which lower the cost of setting up.
Good international links, including ports, airports and broadband, so goods, staff and data can move easily.
Clusters of similar firms and suppliers already in the country, so a new plant can find skilled workers and local suppliers.
Universities and research links with industry, which supply graduates and shared research.
A stable democracy with a pro-business government, which gives a company confidence its investment is safe.
notes.tip: The Ordinary Level question asks for the advantages of Ireland for an MNC. Expected answers are tax, labour, the EU market and IDA, each explained. Do not write 10% for the tax rate, and do not say 12.5% applies to every MNC now.

notes.b: Intel is the main case study. It is a clear example of an MNC whose headquarters and design work stay in the home country while manufacturing is spread across several continents. Intel was founded in 1968, which is earlier than Apple (1976).
points: Intel Corporation was founded in 1968 in California by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore. Its headquarters are in Santa Clara, California, in Silicon Valley (the area of California where many technology companies are based).
Intel made the first commercial microprocessor (a computer's processing chip), the Intel 4004, in 1971.
Intel is best known for the processors inside most personal computers: the x86 family, sold as Pentium and Core, and Xeon for servers (powerful computers that serve other computers).

Wafer fabrication plants ('fabs', factories that make chips on silicon wafers) are at Hillsboro, Oregon (Intel's main research and development fabs); Chandler, Arizona; Rio Rancho, New Mexico; Leixlip, Ireland; and Kiryat Gat, Israel.
Assembly and test plants are at Penang and Kulim in Malaysia, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam, and Chengdu in China.
Sales offices are located around the world, close to the customers they serve.
notes.tip: Do not mix up founding dates: Intel was founded in 1968, Apple in 1976 and Dell in 1984.

notes.b: Ireland's part of Intel is a manufacturing branch plant at Leixlip, Co. Kildare. It is the country's largest private-sector investment.
points: Intel came to Leixlip, Co. Kildare, in 1989.
Its campus is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, with over 30 billion euro invested by 2023. It has several fabs and employs several thousand people.

Fab 34 opened in 2023 and was the first fab in Europe to make chips in high volume using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography (printing the tiny circuit patterns onto the wafer with a very short wavelength of light).
Fab 34 makes the Intel 4 and Intel 3 generations, such as Core Ultra processors.

In 2024 Intel sold a 49% share of the Fab 34 joint venture (a business owned jointly by two companies) to Apollo Global Management, an American investment firm, for about 11 billion US dollars, to raise money for its other projects.
notes.tip: Intel's Leixlip plant makes wafers of processors. Do not say Intel Ireland makes computers, and do not give an exact employment figure, only 'several thousand'.

notes.b: A fab has very particular needs: easy transport, a big site, skilled people and huge supplies of water and electricity. Leixlip met them, which is the answer to the Ordinary question on the advantages of Ireland for Intel.
points: Leixlip is on the M4 motorway west of Dublin, giving road access to the capital, so staff and goods can travel easily.
A large, flat greenfield site, which is undeveloped land, so there was room to build very large plants.
Maynooth University is nearby in Co. Kildare, and Trinity College Dublin and University College Dublin are in the city, giving access to graduates and research links.
A large labour pool in the Dublin area, so Intel can recruit many workers.
A water and electricity supply; fabs use huge amounts of both, so a plant cannot work without a dependable supply.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the advantages of Ireland for the MNC. Tax, labour, the EU market and IDA are the expected answers, and the local site reasons here add detail.

notes.b: For the syllabus you must study one product of the MNC. Intel's product is the microprocessor, and knowing how it is made explains why Intel needs the inputs and locations described next.
points: A microprocessor, or chip, is the 'brain' of a computer, because it carries out the computer's instructions.
It is made by building billions of tiny transistors (tiny electronic switches) in layers on a thin disc of pure silicon called a wafer.
Wafers are processed in a dust-free clean room, because dust would ruin the tiny circuits.

notes.h: Sourcing of raw materials and components
notes.b: Sourcing means where a company gets the materials and parts it needs. A fab depends on a few specialist inputs, and some come from a single supplier.
points: Silicon, refined from quartz sand, is bought as silicon wafers from specialist wafer makers.
Chemicals, specialty gases and metals, which are used up in processing the wafers.
Huge volumes of ultra-pure water and electricity, because the fab uses them continuously.

Manufacturing machines, especially lithography machines (which print the circuit patterns onto wafers) from ASML, based at Veldhoven in the Netherlands. ASML is the only maker of EUV lithography machines, which cost hundreds of millions of euro each.
notes.tip: For the product, name a raw material, such as silicon, and where it or the machines that process it come from.

notes.b: Intel splits chip making into stages and puts each where it suits best. Following the chain from wafer to computer shows how the stages are spread across several continents.
points: 1. Stage 1: wafers are processed in fabs at Leixlip, Hillsboro, Chandler and Kiryat Gat.

2. Stage 2: finished wafers are flown to assembly and test plants in Penang and Kulim (Malaysia), Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) and Chengdu (China), where they are cut into individual chips, packaged and tested.
3. Stage 3: the chips go to computer makers' assembly plants, mostly in Asia.
Chips are small, light and very valuable, so they are moved by air.
The Leixlip plant makes processed wafers only. Cutting, packaging and testing of the chips are not done in Ireland.
notes.tip: The Leixlip plant makes wafers of processors, and the chips are cut, packaged and tested in Asia, not in Ireland.

notes.b: A market is where a product is sold, and a market can be a country, a region or a type of customer. Intel's main customers are computer makers, server makers, governments and businesses.
points: Computer manufacturers are the main customers: Lenovo (China), HP and Dell (USA).
Makers of servers for data centres and cloud computing (storing and running data and programs on remote computers).
Governments and businesses worldwide, because they also buy computers and servers.
Markets are in North America, Europe and Asia, with China one of the largest.
Two markets outside Ireland can be named as countries, for example the USA and China.
notes.tip: A short question asks you to name two markets outside Ireland for the MNC's products. Name countries or regions, such as the USA and China.

notes.b: Intel faces pressures from rivals, costs and supply chains. The exam asks for one difficulty, so learn several to choose from and give each in one explained sentence.
points: Competition from AMD (USA); TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company), the world's largest contract chip maker; Samsung (South Korea); and Nvidia (USA), the leader in chips for artificial intelligence.
Loss of Apple as a customer: Apple began replacing Intel chips in its Mac computers with its own M1 chip in November 2020.
Very high cost of building new fabs.
Falling profits: about 15,000 global job cuts were announced in August 2024, with further cuts in 2025 under the new chief executive, Lip-Bu Tan.
In 2025 the US government took a stake of about 10% in Intel.
Risk that production moves abroad if Ireland's tax advantage narrows (the 15% minimum rate for very large groups) or if costs rise.
High energy costs and pressure on Ireland's electricity grid, since fabs need large amounts of power.
Dependence on Asian supply chains: the global chip shortage of 2021, caused by COVID-19 disruption, halted car and electronics production worldwide.
notes.tip: The Ordinary question asks you to explain a difficulty the MNC faces, now or in future. Expected answers are competition, costs and the risk of relocation. Keep to one sentence per difficulty and do not write a relocation case study here.

notes.b: Intel's presence helps Ireland in several ways. These benefits are described without numbers because no checked figures exist for them.
points: Direct jobs on the Leixlip campus, and indirect (spin-off) jobs with local suppliers and services, which grow because Intel buys goods and services locally.
Corporation tax paid to the State, and exports from the plant.
Skills development and research links with universities.

notes.b: Apple is the alternative case study to Intel. Its product is the iPhone, and it is a good example of a company that designs in one country and has others make its products. Apple was founded in 1976, later than Intel (1968).
points: Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. Its headquarters are at the Apple Park campus in Cupertino, California, which opened in 2017.
Products: the iPhone (2007), iPad (2010), Mac computers and Apple Watch (2015), plus services such as the App Store, iCloud and Apple Music.
Design, software and management are based in California, which makes California the core of the company.

notes.b: Apple's Irish base is in Cork. It is mainly a European headquarters and operations centre, not a phone factory.
points: Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980. It was Apple's first manufacturing plant in Europe.
It employs about 6,000 people in Cork and is Apple's European headquarters.
The Cork campus runs operations and supply chain, finance, and customer support (AppleCare) in many European languages. It also assembles some built-to-order iMac computers.
The Cork campus does not make iPhones.
notes.tip: Apple's Cork campus does not make iPhones. Say only 'about 6,000' for the Cork workforce.

notes.b: Unlike a company that builds everything itself, Apple concentrates on design and management and pays other firms to make its products.
points: Apple owns very little manufacturing itself and outsources production (pays other firms to make its products) to contract manufacturers, which lets it focus on design, software and management.
The chief contract manufacturer is Foxconn (Hon Hai Precision Industry), a Taiwanese company.
Apple runs its own retail stores and an online store.
notes.tip: Foxconn is Taiwanese, not Chinese, though its main plants are in mainland China.

notes.h: The iPhone: sourcing of components and materials
notes.b: An iPhone is built from parts and materials gathered from several countries, so its sourcing is spread across Asia and beyond.
points: Processor chips are designed by Apple and made by TSMC in Taiwan.
Screens are supplied by Samsung and LG (South Korea). Memory and other parts come from other Asian suppliers.
Raw materials include aluminium, lithium and cobalt for batteries, rare earth metals and gold.
Most of the world's cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
notes.tip: TSMC is in Taiwan and Samsung is in South Korea. Do not mix them up.

notes.h: Location of iPhone basic processing units
notes.b: Apple's design is done in California, but the phones are put together elsewhere. Final assembly is concentrated in a few huge plants.
points: Final assembly is done by Foxconn at very large plants in China: Zhengzhou in Henan province, called 'iPhone City', and Shenzhen.
A growing share is assembled in India, around Chennai and Bengaluru, by Foxconn and the Indian Tata group. This reduces dependence on China.
notes.tip: iPhones are assembled by Foxconn and others in China and India, not in Cork.

notes.b: Apple sells its iPhones in almost every region, through its own outlets and through phone companies.
points: iPhones are sold worldwide. The Americas, Europe and China are the largest regions.
Sales are made through Apple Stores, Apple's online store and mobile phone networks.
notes.tip: If asked for two markets outside Ireland, name countries or regions such as the USA and China.

notes.b: Apple has faced legal, supply and reputation problems. As with Intel, one difficulty explained well is what the exam asks for.
points: EU state aid tax case: in 2016 the European Commission ruled that Ireland had given Apple illegal tax benefits worth 13 billion euro, which must be recovered.
The EU General Court overturned the ruling in 2020. In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice reinstated it, and Ireland received about 14 billion euro, including interest.
This was recovery of illegal State aid (help from a government that gives a company an unfair advantage), which is unpaid tax, not a fine. Ireland had argued against collecting it.
Dependence on China for assembly, and trade tensions between the USA and China.
Competition from Samsung and from Chinese phone makers, which can take customers from Apple.
Criticism of working conditions in supplier factories, which can harm Apple's reputation.
Athenry, Co. Galway: Apple announced a data centre (about 850 million euro) in 2015 and abandoned it in 2018 after planning and appeal delays.
notes.tip: Do not call the Apple tax case a fine. It was recovery of illegal State aid, which is unpaid tax, and Ireland had argued against collecting it.

notes.h: Skill: locating an MNC on an Ordnance Survey map
notes.b: Use map evidence to justify a location, and give one reason against a location. The map question asks for two reasons an MNC might locate in a mapped area, with map evidence, and one reason against.
points: Look for transport: a motorway, national primary road, railway, port or airport, because an MNC needs to move goods and staff.
Look for a large, flat site, shown by widely spaced contours (the lines joining points of equal height; wide spacing means gentle slopes).
Look for a nearby town for labour and services, and for an industrial estate symbol, which shows land already set aside for industry.
Look for a water supply, such as a river or lake, because industry needs water.
Reasons against a site: steep or flood-prone land (closely spaced contours or marsh), poor roads, a remote location, or protected scenery.

Invented illustration, not a real map: a flat site beside a motorway junction, a market town nearby and a river for water. Each point should give the feature, the location and the reason it suits an MNC.
notes.tip: Give two reasons with map evidence and one reason against. Each point should name the feature, say where it is on the map and say why it suits an MNC.

notes.h: Skill: data response on the largest MNCs
notes.b: A data response may give a chart or table of the largest MNCs by value. You are then asked to draw a bar chart and calculate differences.
points: Draw a bar chart with one bar per company, a labelled value axis starting at zero, and units in the title, so the bars can be compared fairly.
Calculate a difference by subtracting the smaller value from the larger, and state the answer with its units.
The method is set out in the note Tables, Graphs and Data Skills.
notes.tip: Expect to draw a bar chart and calculate differences from a chart or table of the largest MNCs by value.

keyTerms.definition: A company with its headquarters in a home country and production or service branches in several host countries.
Another name for a multinational company.
Investment by a company in another country through building or buying a plant there.
The State agency that attracts and supports foreign direct investment in Ireland.
A thin disc of pure silicon on which the layers of a microprocessor are built.
A wafer fabrication plant where the circuits of microprocessors are made on silicon wafers.
A chip made of billions of transistors that acts as the brain of a computer.
Extreme ultraviolet lithography, the process of printing circuits onto silicon wafers with very short wavelength light.
A company that assembles products for other companies, such as Foxconn for Apple.

factCards.term: Typical structure and organisation of a multinational company
factCards.definition: Headquarters, R&D and top management stay in the home country (the core); branch plants, regional headquarters and sales offices are abroad. Decisions are made at headquarters, and branch plants compete with each other inside the company for investment.

factCards.term: MNC production stages: what they are and how they are spread
factCards.definition: Design and R&D; basic processing of raw materials and components; assembly and testing; distribution and sales. Each stage is placed wherever it is cheapest or most efficient, which spreads sourcing, processing and markets across the world.

factCards.term: Why multinationals choose Ireland: give eight advantages
factCards.definition: Low corporation tax (12.5%; 15% for very large groups from 2024); a young, educated, English-speaking workforce; EU single market access, and since Brexit the only mainly English-speaking euro country; IDA grants; ports, airports and broadband; clusters; universities; stability.

factCards.term: IDA Ireland: role, size and why FDI concentrates around Dublin
factCards.definition: Set up in 1949 to attract and keep foreign direct investment. Client firms employ about 300,000 people in about 1,800 companies (2023–24), concentrated in Dublin and the Mid-East: the largest labour pool, universities, Dublin Port and Airport, services and existing clusters.

factCards.term: Intel: founding, founders, headquarters and products
factCards.definition: Founded in 1968 in California by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore; headquarters Santa Clara, in Silicon Valley. It made the first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004, in 1971, and makes the x86 processors in most personal computers (Pentium, Core; Xeon for servers).

factCards.term: Intel in Leixlip, Co. Kildare: key facts
factCards.definition: Came in 1989; Ireland's largest private-sector investment (over €30 billion by 2023), with several fabs and several thousand staff. Fab 34 (2023) was Europe's first high-volume EUV chip fab. In 2024 Intel sold 49% of the Fab 34 venture to Apollo for about $11 billion.

factCards.term: Why Intel chose Leixlip: local site factors
factCards.definition: On the M4 west of Dublin, within reach of Dublin Airport and Port; a large, flat greenfield site; Maynooth University nearby, with Trinity College Dublin and University College Dublin in the city; a large Dublin labour pool; water and electricity, used in huge amounts.

factCards.term: Intel microprocessor: sourcing of raw materials and components
factCards.definition: Silicon wafers (silicon refined from quartz sand) bought from specialist wafer makers; chemicals, specialty gases and metals; huge volumes of ultra-pure water and electricity; machines, especially EUV lithography machines from ASML of Veldhoven, Netherlands, the only maker.

factCards.term: Intel microprocessor: location of basic processing units
factCards.definition: Wafers are processed in fabs at Leixlip, Hillsboro (Oregon), Chandler (Arizona) and Kiryat Gat (Israel), then flown to Penang and Kulim (Malaysia), Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) and Chengdu (China) to be cut, packaged and tested. Chips are light and valuable, so they go by air.

factCards.term: Intel microprocessor: location of its markets
factCards.definition: Computer makers such as Lenovo (China), HP and Dell (USA); makers of servers for data centres and cloud computing; governments and businesses worldwide. Markets are in North America, Europe and Asia, with China one of the largest.

Competition from AMD, TSMC, Samsung and Nvidia; Apple switched Macs to its own M1 chip from 2020; very costly new fabs; falling profits and about 15,000 global job cuts (2024); a narrowing Irish tax advantage; high energy costs; reliance on Asian supply chains (2021 chip shortage).

factCards.term: Intel: benefits of its Leixlip plant to Ireland
factCards.definition: Direct jobs on the Leixlip campus and spin-off jobs with local suppliers and services; corporation tax paid to the State; exports; skills development and research links with universities.

factCards.term: Apple: founding, founders, headquarters and products
factCards.definition: Founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak; headquarters Apple Park, Cupertino, California (opened 2017). Products: iPhone (2007), iPad (2010), Mac, Apple Watch (2015) and services such as the App Store and iCloud. Design, software and management stay in California.

factCards.term: Apple in Cork: what the Hollyhill campus does
factCards.definition: Opened in 1980 as Apple's first European manufacturing plant; now its European headquarters with about 6,000 staff. It runs operations and supply chain, finance and multilingual AppleCare support, and assembles some built-to-order iMacs. It does not make iPhones.

factCards.term: iPhone: sourcing of components and raw materials
factCards.definition: Chips designed by Apple and made by TSMC in Taiwan; screens from Samsung and LG (South Korea); memory from other Asian suppliers; aluminium, lithium and cobalt for batteries (most cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo), rare earth metals and gold.

factCards.term: iPhone: basic processing units and markets
factCards.definition: Apple outsources assembly to Foxconn, a Taiwanese contract manufacturer, at Zhengzhou ('iPhone City') and Shenzhen in China; a growing share is assembled near Chennai and Bengaluru, India (Foxconn, Tata). Largest markets: the Americas, Europe and China.

factCards.term: Apple and the EU state-aid tax case: the timeline
factCards.definition: 2016: the European Commission ruled Ireland had given Apple illegal tax benefits worth €13 billion. 2020: the EU General Court overturned this. September 2024: the EU Court of Justice reinstated it; Ireland received about €14 billion with interest. Unpaid tax, not a fine.

factCards.term: Apple: other difficulties and issues it faces
factCards.definition: Dependence on China for assembly amid US–China trade tensions; competition from Samsung and Chinese phone makers; criticism of supplier working conditions; the Athenry data centre (about €850 million), announced 2015, abandoned 2018 after planning delays.

questions.prompt: With reference to one multinational company you have studied, examine the sourcing of raw materials and components, the location of its basic processing units and the location of its markets for one of its products.
questions.model: Company and product: Intel and the microprocessor. Sourcing: silicon, refined from quartz sand, is bought as silicon wafers from specialist makers, with chemicals, specialty gases and metals. Intel uses huge volumes of ultra-pure water and electricity. Its lithography machines come from ASML in the Netherlands, the only maker of EUV machines. Basic processing: wafers are processed in fabs at Leixlip in Ireland, Hillsboro in Oregon, Chandler in Arizona and Kiryat Gat in Israel. Finished wafers are flown to assembly and test plants in Penang and Kulim in Malaysia, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam and Chengdu in China, where they are cut, packaged and tested. The chips are light and valuable, so they are moved by air. Markets: the chips go to computer makers, mostly in Asia, such as Lenovo in China, and to HP and Dell in the USA. Intel also sells chips for servers in data centres and cloud computing. Its markets are in North America, Europe and Asia, with China one of the largest. Governments and businesses worldwide buy its products. Conclusion of the location pattern: the stages are spread across the world to where each is cheapest or most efficient, and Ireland's role is the wafer-processing stage.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one multinational company you have studied and where it is located in Ireland. (ii) Name one raw material it uses and one product it makes. (iii) Explain two advantages of an Irish location for this company. (iv) Explain one difficulty it faces.
questions.model: (i) Apple, at Hollyhill in Cork. (ii) Aluminium, or cobalt for batteries, is a raw material; the product is the iPhone. (iii) First, Ireland has a low corporation tax of 12.5%, which makes Cork attractive to a company with large profits; the tax rate rises to 15% only for very large groups. Second, Cork has an educated, English-speaking and multilingual workforce, so the company can run its European headquarters and customer support in many European languages from Cork, and it has about 6,000 staff there. Ireland's membership of the EU also gives access to the single market. (iv) One difficulty is dependence on China for assembly, since Foxconn's main iPhone plants are in China. Trade tensions between the USA and China make this supply chain risky, and Apple is shifting some assembly to India to reduce the risk. The Cork campus does not make iPhones, so the difficulty is about the product's supply chain, not Cork.

questions.prompt: Explain the term multinational company and describe its typical structure.
questions.model: A multinational company is a company with its headquarters in a home country and production or service branches in several other countries, called host countries. Its typical structure has headquarters, research and development and top management in the home country, forming the core. Branch plants and sales offices are placed in other countries. Intel shows this pattern: its headquarters are in Santa Clara, California, its main research fabs are in Hillsboro, Oregon, and it runs fabs and assembly plants in Ireland, Israel, Malaysia, Vietnam and China. Decisions are made at headquarters, and branch plants compete with each other for investment.
